# Core exercise: more seedlings, how much uncertainty?

| | |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Use the updating calculation to explain how sample size changes uncertainty about seedling survival. |
| **Computation** | A grid approximation, plotted with ggplot2. No external R files, saved fits or Stan are needed. |
| **Model** | Survivors $y \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(N,p)$, with $p \sim \operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$. |

The slides used coin tosses and a strong prior to illustrate how data and a prior
combine. Here the unknown probability is seedling survival. We use the same
binomial structure, with a flat prior, and calculate the update ourselves.

## 1. Read the calculation for 2 survivors out of 5

Run the supplied code. `y` is the number surviving; `N` is the number surveyed.
`p` lists possible values of the unknown survival probability.

```{r core-data-comparison, fig.height=3.4}
y <- 2
N <- 5
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 501)

prior <- dbeta(p, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1)
likelihood <- dbinom(x = y, size = N, prob = p)
posterior <- prior * likelihood
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)

tibble(p = p, posterior = posterior) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = posterior)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#d95f02") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 0.02)) +
  labs(x = "Survival probability p",
       y = "Posterior probability per grid point",
       title = paste(y, "survivors out of", N, "seedlings"))
```

`dbeta()` gives the prior density at each candidate `p`. Beta(1,1) gives equal
prior weight across these candidates. `dbinom()` gives the probability of the
observed count for each candidate `p`: this is the likelihood.
Multiplication combines them; the last calculation makes the weights sum to 1.
This is a discrete approximation on an equally spaced grid. The plotted heights
are probabilities assigned to grid points, rather than a continuous density.

With your partner, point to the line that represents each part of
**posterior $\propto$ prior $\times$ likelihood**.
You can use the plotting code as supplied.

## 2. Predict, change the counts, then check

Imagine surveying 100 seedlings and finding 40 survivors.

**Before running anything:** will the posterior be wider or narrower?
Will the observed survival proportion change?

Change only `y <- 2` to `y <- 40` and `N <- 5` to `N <- 100` in the code above,
then rerun the whole chunk. Keep the prior, grid and plot axes unchanged.
Use the earlier figure in this HTML as a reference for the 2/5 case.
Swap who runs the code and who explains the figure.

Write one sentence: **“The observed survival proportion stays at …, but …”**
Use the width of the posterior to support your explanation.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

Assume participants can run supplied R code and edit two assignments; do not
require function writing or a derivation of the Beta posterior. Allow about
8 minutes for reading, prediction, editing and discussion, then 4 for explanation.
If time is short, skip the optional prior comparison below.

`prior <- dbeta(...)` supplies the prior; `likelihood <- dbinom(...)` evaluates
the likelihood with the counts fixed and p varying; multiplication and
normalisation produce the grid posterior. The plotting lines only display it.

Both observed proportions are 0.4. The continuous posteriors approximated here
are Beta(3,4) and Beta(41,61); the second is narrower. Example explanation:
“The observed survival proportion stays at 0.4, but the larger survey gives a
narrower posterior and less uncertainty about the survival probability.”
The means are 3/7 and 41/102, so do not claim that their means are identical.
A narrower distribution does not mean that survival itself has become less
variable or that the model assumptions have been verified.

The grid and vertical limits are identical, so widths and heights are comparable.
The y-axis is probability per grid point: changing the grid would change those
heights. Do not confuse them with a continuous density.

:::
:::

# Optional extension: change the prior

Return to `y <- 2` and `N <- 5`. Change only the prior line to:

```{r optional-prior, eval=FALSE}
prior <- dbeta(p, shape1 = 8, shape2 = 2)
```

Beta(8,2) gives more prior weight to high survival probabilities.
Predict which way the posterior will move, then rerun the whole calculation
with this replacement. Keep the data, grid and plot axes fixed.
What earlier ecological evidence could support that prior?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

The continuous posterior is Beta(10,5), with mean 10/15, compared with 3/7 under
the flat prior. The posterior shifts towards higher survival probabilities.
These priors are teaching contrasts, not general recommendations; a high-survival
prior needs evidence from a comparable habitat and census period.

:::
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}

# Instructor demonstration: Stan reads the same model

This is a demonstration after the core exercise. Follow the mapping from data to
unknown survival probability and assumptions. Running these chunks is optional.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(patchwork)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))
source(here("R/course_utils.R"))
source(here("R/course_visuals.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size=14))
```

```{r demo-stan, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
cat("```stan\n", paste(readLines(here("stan/binomial.stan")), collapse="\n"), "\n```\n", sep="")
```

```{r demo-draws}
fit <- course_fit("day1_seedling")
draws <- fit$draws
fit$source
plot_update(2, 5, 1, 1) +
  geom_histogram(data=as_tibble(draws), aes(x=p, y=after_stat(density)),
                 inherit.aes=FALSE, bins=30, fill="grey40", alpha=.2)
```

The histogram approximates the exact posterior curve. Stan returns samples from
a distribution. It does not return only a best value. The saved result uses the
same 2/5 data and Beta(1,1) prior as our first plot.

## The same model in brms

brms writes Stan code from an R formula. Here we keep exactly the same model:

$$y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(5,p),\qquad p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1).$$

Read this as an alternative way to specify the model within the same demonstration,
not an additional exercise. These chunks are not run when building the handout.
The saved Stan result above remains the classroom fallback; it is not a brms fit.

```{r demo-brms-model, eval=FALSE}
library(brms)
seedlings <- data.frame(y=2L, N=5L)
seedling_formula <- bf(y | trials(N) ~ 0 + Intercept)
seedling_family <- binomial(link="identity")
seedling_prior <- set_prior("beta(1, 1)", class="b", lb=0, ub=1)
```

| Part of the model | Stan | brms |
|---|---|---|
| Observed counts | `N=5`, `y=2` | One row of `seedlings`; `trials(N)` supplies the number of seedlings |
| Unknown probability | `p`, bounded between 0 and 1 | `0 + Intercept` gives one coefficient, bounded by `lb=0, ub=1` |
| Observation model | `y ~ binomial(N, p)` | `binomial(link="identity")` makes that coefficient equal to $p$ |
| Prior | `p ~ beta(1, 1)` | The Beta prior on this coefficient, `class="b"` |

`0 + Intercept` treats the intercept as an ordinary coefficient so that the bounded
prior applies to it. With the identity link, this coefficient is the probability
itself. This bounded, intercept-only example matches our Stan model. The usual
logit link instead models log-odds; a Normal prior there would give a different
prior on $p$. Day 2 uses that logit formulation for a density-dependent probability.

**Optional instructor execution:** run the following only in a prepared environment
with brms, CmdStan and a working C++ toolchain. It compiles a new model and runs new
inference; participants do not need to run it or install anything. Prepare the result
before class rather than waiting for compilation during the demonstration.

```{r demo-brms-fit, eval=FALSE}
fit_brms <- brm(
  formula=seedling_formula, data=seedlings,
  family=seedling_family, prior=seedling_prior,
  backend="cmdstanr", seed=20261021,
  chains=4, cores=2, iter=2000, warmup=1000, refresh=0
)
brms_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit_brms)
p_brms <- brms_draws$b_Intercept  # identity link: this is p, not logit(p)
mean(p_brms)
quantile(p_brms, c(0.05, 0.95))

plot_update(2, 5, 1, 1) +
  geom_histogram(data=data.frame(p=p_brms), aes(x=p, y=after_stat(density)),
                 inherit.aes=FALSE, bins=30, fill="grey40", alpha=.2)
```

The target posterior is again Beta(3,4): mean $3/7$ and the same exact interval as
the first plot. The brms and handwritten Stan histograms should approximate the
same distribution; individual draws and summaries need not match exactly.
Before using a new fit, inspect chain traces, R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, divergences,
treedepth and E-BFMI together. Model checking is still needed beyond computation.

For an optional look at the generated Stan code, without compilation or sampling:

```{r demo-brms-stancode, eval=FALSE}
cat(make_stancode(seedling_formula, data=seedlings,
                  family=seedling_family, prior=seedling_prior))
```

References: brms documentation on [formulas](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brmsformula.html),
[bounded priors](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/set_prior.html),
and [supported links](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brmsfamily.html).

# Optional extension: a numerical summary

Do this after the core exercise or after class. The data and model stay fixed.

```{r optional-summary}
draws <- course_fit("day1_seedling")$draws
summarise_update(2, 5, 1, 1)
mean(draws$p)
quantile(draws$p, c(0.05, 0.95))
mean(draws$p > 0.5)
```

Interpret the interval in words. What does the last line estimate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

The interval describes uncertainty about the survival probability, conditional on
the model, prior and data. The final line approximates the posterior probability
that $p>0.5$. Small differences between the exact Beta calculations and saved
Stan draws reflect Monte Carlo approximation. These summaries are optional today.

:::

:::

# Reflection

What does the posterior width tell you that the observed proportion alone does not?
On Day 2 we keep the binomial model and let survival probability depend on density.
